The Japanese concept of *wabi-sabi*—finding beauty in impermanence and imperfection—gets thrown around like incense at wellness retreats now. Which is adorable, really. Because the same people quoting Rumi about cracks letting light in will also DM a stranger asking why they didn't Photoshop out their laugh lines.

We don't want the broken thing itself. We want the sanitized version of brokenness. The curated ruin. The aesthetically pleasing failure that doesn't make anyone uncomfortable.

Which brings me to what's actually happening here. This whole conversation about finding beauty in flaws is code for permission. Permission to stop performing constant improvement. Permission to let things wear. Permission to show up unvarnished without being punished for it (at least online).

captions.instagram:
Stop glorifying brokenness—here's why it's a lazy excuse.

Look, I get it. There's something almost noble in finding aesthetic value in cracked porcelain, in rusted-out machinery, in lives half-lived. It’s the artistic equivalent of eating expired yogurt because at least you’re being *authentic*. But let me be your designated hater here: this whole "beauty in brokenness" thing is a scam we sell ourselves when actually fixing things seems too much work.

We love broken things as long as they stay broken. We take pictures of peeling paint but God forbid you suggest scraping it off and repainting. We write profound essays about our wounds while actively refusing therapy. We fetishize the patina of decay because maintenance is boring and expensive.

And sure, there IS something beautiful in scars—*after* healing has occurred. A healed scar tells a story of survival. An unhealed wound is just gross. That crack in your vase isn't beautiful because it's cracked; it's beautiful because someone carefully mended it with gold (a practice called kintsukai where literally everything gets gilded over). You don't celebrate the shatter. You celebrate what was done with the pieces afterward.

So maybe instead of flipping the script entirely from "perfection" to "imperfect," we could try something radical: how about *functionality*?

A perfectly working toilet is more beautiful than a beautifully decorated one that doesn't flush. A reliably running car is more gorgeous than one covered in meaningful rust patterns. A relationship that actually meets both people's needs beats a dramatically tragic one by every measurable standard except Instagram engagement.

captions.instagram:
Let me tell you about intentions—the most overrated currency we have.

I'm sitting here thinking about my own cascading failure engine, which started with something so beautifully mundane it's almost pathetic: I intended to be *interesting*. That was it. Just one little spark of ego, right around age 28, when I realized that being competent wasn't enough. People wanted to see me burn, but brighter than anyone else was burning.

This is where things get delicious because an intention isn't some pure, noble thing. It's a seed with its own built-in rot factor. My "intention" to be interesting immediately required performance, which meant I had to notice what people responded to—so now I'm monitoring reactions instead of just doing work. That attention-seeking became addiction (a classic cascade step). Addiction requires novelty, so I stopped finishing projects and kept starting new ones. Now my resume looks like a scattershot of half-completed brilliances rather than singular mastery—a reputation as someone who has many great starts but no endings.

But wait, there's more! Because I needed these novel ideas to seem profound, I began reading broadly across disciplines without actually mastering any. This created a surface-level fluency that made me dangerous at parties but shallow in practice. I developed what I thought was a unique perspective but was really just a pastiche of other people's deeper thoughts. When called upon to execute, I'd flounder because my understanding was all aesthetic and no substance...

Share this with someone who needs it.

#TheNineStitches #CognitiveBias #SelfUnderstanding #InnerWorkJourney

I thought being “interesting” would make me a better parent, but it turned my life into a series of half‑finished projects.  

At 28 I decided I needed constant attention—more likes, more applause, more novelty. That intention quickly became a habit. I started measuring every reaction, chasing the next spark instead of finishing what I’d started.  

The result? A résumé that reads like a list of ideas that never landed. I read wildly across topics, hoping breadth would mask the lack of depth. It made me sound clever at gatherings, but when real work showed up, I was stuck.  

For my kids, that pattern meant I was always “on” with new apps, gadgets, or trends, never fully exploring any one thing. The excitement faded fast, and the deeper, quieter moments—reading together, building a project from start to finish—were lost.

captions.instagram:
Staying vs. growing—here's a truth nobody talks about. Real reflection doesn't push you forward OR hold you back. It just complicates things by turning your autopilots into conscious decisions. Suddenly you see YOURSELF in situations you used to blame others for. So now what?

I've learned to tell the difference between productive rumination ("what am I learning?") and toxic dwelling ("why is everyone happier?"). One builds insight. The Other builds therapy bills.

Change isn't some heroic 2AM tweet. Sometimes you just gotta sit with discomfort before anything meaningful shifts. 🍕
